title: Bethel and the Jabbok
lead: A man running from the consequences of his own mistakes can meet the God who transforms people who have fought all their lives.
questions: If God asked you tonight what your name is, what truth about yourself would you finally have to say out loud?
Which parts of your faith are still an inherited story rather than your own Bethel?
Whom have you wronged and keep avoiding, even though the road back to God runs through making peace with them?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Jacob didn’t wait for the blessing. He stole it: he took advantage of his brother’s hunger and lied to his blind father. And when it all came out, he ran. He spends his first night under the open sky with a stone for a pillow. And right there, at the least holy moment of his life, God finds him. He doesn’t say, “Once you’ve cleaned up your act, we’ll talk.” He says, “Look, I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go.” A sentence that Adam never heard, nor Noah, nor Abraham, is spoken to a runaway cheat.

In a dream Jacob sees a ladder reaching from earth to heaven. The tower of Babel was a staircase built from the bottom up, and it never reached its goal. Here the stairway is let down from above, for a sleeping man who hadn’t asked for anything. And God doesn’t stand far off at the top: the LORD stood over him, bending over a weary man. In the morning Jacob says, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.” He grew up surrounded by stories about God, but only that night did he meet Him personally. Inherited religion and a living relationship are not the same thing.

Twenty years later he sets out for home, and the Bible again says he “fled,” this time from Laban. Across the Jabbok, Esau is waiting with four hundred men. In the night “a man wrestled with him until daybreak.” The account of the struggle contains an almost unbelievable sentence: “the man saw that he could not overpower Jacob.” Yet a single touch was enough to dislocate his hip. God could have won at any moment. He didn’t, because He wanted Jacob, for the first time, to give up. And for the first time Jacob has no scheme left; he only pleads: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”

But his opponent asks, “What is your name?” Twenty years earlier, when his father asked the same question, Jacob lied: I am Esau. Now he tells the truth: Jacob, the one who grabs the heel. He confesses everything. Only then does the blessing come, along with a new name: Israel. In the morning, limping, he goes out to meet his brother first, ahead of the whole camp. Esau runs to him, throws his arms around his neck, and they both weep. And Jacob says, “I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God.” The road to the Almighty led through reconciliation with the brother he had wronged.

Until now we have been reading about people who waited for the promise. Jacob is different. He stole the blessing. He took advantage of his brother’s hunger, lied to his blind father, disguised himself as someone he wasn’t. And when it all came out, he packed up and ran. Today’s reading is two nights in the life of a con man: the first at the start of his flight, the second twenty years later, on the way home. Between the two, God will do something in Jacob that neither his father’s blessing, nor his wealth, nor his family ever did.

sections.heading: A Bed No One Offered Him
paragraphs: “On reaching a certain place, he spent the night there because the sun had set. And taking one of the stones from that place, he put it under his head.” In that part of the world, travelers caught out by nightfall were often taken in, but the text doesn’t tell us whether Jacob looked for a place to stay. All we know is that a son from a wealthy home is sleeping under the open sky with a stone under his head. A long road lies ahead of him, and behind him, a flight after a fraud.

And right there, at the least holy moment of his life, God finds him. It’s worth saying as carefully as possible, because all of today’s hope lives in this sentence: God meets Jacob not after his conversion but in the middle of his flight after a fraud. He doesn’t say, “We’ll talk once you’ve cleaned up your act.” He says, “Look, I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go.” Adam didn’t hear that sentence in the garden, nor Noah at the ark, nor Abraham at his calling. In all of Genesis, God says it directly to only two people: quiet Isaac, heir of the promise, and Jacob, a runaway cheat on the first night of his escape. Apparently this sentence is not a reward for a good résumé.

sections.heading: A Stairway Let Down from Above
paragraphs: In his dream Jacob sees “a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven.” The ancient world knew images like this well, only running in the opposite direction. The ziggurats of Mesopotamia were exactly that: stairways to heaven, structures by which humans were meant to climb up into the realm of the gods. Babel wanted “a tower that reaches to the heavens,” and it ended in scattering. At Bethel we have the same picture and the opposite direction: no one builds these stairs from the ground up. They are let down from above, for a sleeping man who hadn’t asked for anything.

Babel means “gate of god.” People built themselves a gate to heaven that never became a gate. And the phrase “the gate of heaven” occurs only once in the entire Hebrew Bible: here, at Bethel, over a fugitive with a stone under his head, without a single brick of human making. Access to God is not the prize of a climb. It is a gift that comes down. Centuries later Jesus will complete this scene when He tells Nathanael about the angels of God “ascending and descending on the Son of Man.” The ladder of Bethel will turn out to be a Person.

And where is God in this dream? Not at the top of the ladder, distant and out of reach. The text can be read to say that the LORD stood over him, over the sleeping man. Bending over a weary man like someone keeping watch at a bedside. From there come the promises: the land, descendants, blessing for all the families of the earth, and finally the most urgent thing of all: protection at every step of the way and the promise of a return home. Jacob will bring up food and clothing himself in the morning, in his vow to the Creator, and he will receive those, too. The Lord of great promises turns out to be the same God who knows a fugitive is worried about tomorrow’s meal.

sections.heading: And I Was Unaware of It
paragraphs: Jacob’s reaction when he wakes up is priceless: “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.” Jacob grew up in a home where people talked about God. He knew his grandfather’s stories; he had heard his father’s prayers. And yet only this night, alone, on a stone, does he stand before God in his own name, and it terrifies him. Inherited religion and a relationship of your own are not the same thing. You can spend your whole life one step away from Bethel and never know it. In every church there are people who know all the stories secondhand and are waiting, often without realizing it, for their first night with a stone under their head.

The vow Jacob makes in the morning sounds like a bargain: if You will be with me, if You give me food, if I return safely, then You will be my God. But read carefully, it largely repeats what the Creator has just promised: You will be with me, You will watch over me, I will return to this land. Jacob prays with words he has just heard, because he doesn’t have any of his own yet. At the start of the journey, that is enough. And the Bible will not keep a careful record of whether Jacob kept every item of his vow. It will, however, carefully hold the Almighty to His promises. Holy Scripture keeps an account of God’s faithfulness, not ours.

sections.heading: Twenty Years Later
paragraphs: The second night comes on the way back. Jacob returns a wealthy man: two wives, eleven children, flocks and herds. His return is described with the same verb as his departure: the text says that he “fled” from Laban. Twenty years have passed, and Jacob is still a man on the run. Ahead of him is the Jabbok River, and beyond the river, Esau with four hundred men. The past he has been running from for two decades is waiting on the other bank.

That evening Jacob begins his prayer with words he has never spoken before: “I am unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown Your servant.” The man who has spent his life taking now counts up: “with only my staff I came across the Jordan, but now I have become two camps.” For the first time he sees his wealth not as winnings but as an undeserved gift. That is already the beginning of a transformation. But the most important part is still to come.

sections.heading: Wrestling Until Daybreak
paragraphs: “So Jacob was left all alone, and there a man wrestled with him until daybreak.” We don’t know how the fight began, and we can’t see it clearly, because it happens in the dark: the reader is not allowed to see more than Jacob saw. What we do know is how it ended, and that ending is one of the strangest sentences in Scripture: “When the man saw that he could not overpower Jacob, he struck the socket of Jacob’s hip.” Could not overpower him? One touch was enough to dislocate his hip. The one wrestling with Jacob could have won at any moment. He didn’t want to. In this struggle God limits His own strength, because He isn’t interested in defeating Jacob but in something else: getting Jacob to stop winning.

There is one more tender detail in this struggle. It isn’t Jacob who asks first. His opponent asks first: “Let me go, for it is daybreak.” The stronger asks the weaker to let Him go. Some read it this way: daylight would reveal His face, and no one can see God and live. God asks to be released in order to save the one who is holding on to Him.

And sure enough, only when he has been beaten by a single touch, clinging to his opponent because his leg will no longer hold him, does Jacob do what he has never done before: he asks. “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” The same stubbornness with which he had grabbed, stolen, and schemed turns in the right direction for the first time. Two blessings in his life he won by trickery. The third he begs for, beaten and lame. And it is that third one that is worth the most.

sections.heading: What Is Your Name?
paragraphs: Instead of blessing him right away, the opponent asks a question: “What is your name?” This is not a request for personal details. Twenty years earlier, in a dark tent, his blind father asked Jacob the same thing, and he answered, “I am Esau.” His whole life rested on that lie. Now, in a different darkness, the question comes back. And for the first time Jacob tells the truth: “Jacob.” That name meant something like “the one who grabs the heel,” a schemer. To say it out loud was to confess everything. The blessing comes only after that confession. God can work with a cheat who tells Him his real name. He can’t work with a fake Esau.

Jacob asks for a name, too: “Please tell me your name.” Instead of a name he gets a question, “Why do you ask my name?”, and a blessing. Centuries later Samson’s father will hear the same thing: “Why do you ask my name… since it is beyond comprehension?” And when Moses asks the same question, he will be given a name that no definition can contain: “I AM WHO I AM.” So God doesn’t refuse Jacob out of distrust. He refuses because He doesn’t want to be just a name for Jacob to remember. The Lord gives Jacob Himself, not information about Himself. That’s a good pattern for our prayers, too: fewer explanations, more presence.

The new name is Israel. The text explains it with the words “you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed.” The name is also sometimes read as “God fights.” Perhaps that double meaning is the point: a whole nation will carry in its name the memory of the night a man wrestled with God, and the promise that from now on the Lord fights for him. Jacob comes out of that night with a dislocated hip, limping. A strange victory: the winner limps, and his only trophy is a wound. But that wound is the blessing, because from that night on Jacob will never be self-sufficient again. “The sun rose above him as he passed by Penuel, and he was limping because of his hip.” He fled at sunset. He comes back at sunrise.

sections.heading: The Second Face
paragraphs: He still has to cross the river and meet his brother. For twenty years Jacob hid behind others. This morning, limping, he steps out in front of his whole camp and goes first. And Esau, whom we last saw plotting murder, “ran to him and embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. And they both wept.” Anyone who knows the parable of the prodigal son will recognize every gesture.

Then Jacob says something to his brother that ties his two nights together: “I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God.” Penuel means “face of God.” Within a single day Jacob saw the face of the Lord twice: once in the night struggle, and once in the face of the brother who forgave him. These two encounters cannot be separated. Jacob’s road back to God led straight through reconciliation with the man he had wronged. That order can rarely be rearranged: whoever has a wronged brother waiting across the river usually still has their own struggle at the Jabbok ahead of them.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: God met Jacob twice, and both times at the wrong moment: once in the middle of his flight after a fraud, once on the night before the confrontation Jacob feared most. Not once did He wait for the man to improve. Nor did He ever leave him the way He found him. That is the pattern for today, for us and for the people we have given up on: God receives people in the middle of their flight and does not require them to improve before He meets them. Transformation is not the ticket in. It is the result of the encounter.
